summary: For ages 9–11, build the interlocking ideas of factors (numbers that divide into a whole), multiples (a number's times table), and what two numbers share in common (common factors and common multiples). Learners search factor pairs systematically (pairing 1,2,3… and stopping near the square root), sharply distinguish factor from multiple, and treat 'common' as the overlap of two sets. Work is grounded in problems and linked downstream to simplifying fractions, finding common denominators, and later HCF/LCM and ratio. A manipulable sets-and-overlap tool is proposed as the core builder, with a two-tier probe and a static reference/quiz as complementary assessment and scaffolds.
misconceptions: Confusing factors with multiples (factor of 12 vs multiple of 12).
Missing factor pairs through unsystematic searching, especially middle ones and the number itself/1.
Thinking there is a 'largest multiple' or a 'smallest factor other than 1' confusion.
Treating 'common' loosely rather than as shared between BOTH numbers.
Forgetting 1 is a common factor of every pair, or that the numbers themselves are factors.

activities.title: Factors-and-multiples explorer (three linked modes)
steps: Factor mode: for a chosen number N (e.g. 36), form every possible rectangle (array) of N counters and log each pair of side-lengths as a factor pair on a factor rainbow — e.g. (1,36), (2,18), (3,12), (4,9), (6,6).
Explain how you know you have found them all: pairs are logged from the outside in, and once you reach the square root the pairs repeat, so the set is complete.

Multiple mode: set one number line to skip-count in 7 and read off the first five multiples (7,14,21,28,35); then set two adjustable number lines to skip-count in 6 and 8, watch where the hops coincide, and record the first THREE common multiples (24, 48, 72) — the first collision is at 24.

Common mode: set two numbers (e.g. 24 and 36), pour each factor list into a two-set Venn diagram, slide the shared factors into the overlap, and identify the largest shared factor (12) as the highest common factor; then repeat with 36 and 48 (shared factors 1,2,3,4,6,12, highest common factor 12).
State in words what 'common' means here: a factor or multiple shared by BOTH numbers — the intersection of the two sets.
activities.insight: 'Common' literally means the overlap of two sets; completeness of a factor list comes from systematic pairing around the square root; and the first common multiple is the first place two skip-counts collide. Factors are finite and divide into a number (rectangle side-lengths), while multiples are infinite times-table hops.

activities.title: Factor detective: prove the list is complete
steps: For a given number, argue aloud or in writing that no factor has been missed: test divisibility in order (1, 2, 3, …) and pair each factor with its partner.
Justify why you can stop checking near the square root: if N = a×b, one of a or b is at most √N, so any larger factor has already appeared as a partner.
Identify what two chosen numbers share and defend your answer: which factors (and which early multiples) belong to BOTH?
activities.insight: Systematic searching plus the square-root stopping point guarantees a complete factor list, and 'common' must be justified as membership in both sets.

activities.title: Is it prime? Decide and justify the stopping point
steps: Decide whether a given number (e.g. 97) is prime.
Test divisibility only by primes up to the square root (for 97: 2, 3, 5, 7, since √97 ≈ 9.8) and record the results.
Explain WHY you can stop at about 10: beyond √97 any factor would pair with one already checked.
Conclude using the definition: a prime has exactly two distinct factors (1 and itself); 1 is neither prime nor composite because it has only one factor.
activities.insight: Primeness is about the NUMBER of factors, not about being odd; factor-pairing around the square root tells you when it is safe to stop checking.

activities.title: Static reference and checking quiz
steps: Study a factor rainbow of 36 and an adjacent Venn of the factors of 24 and 36, tapping to reveal the common factors.
Sort items into 'factor of 24' vs 'multiple of 24' to rehearse the core discrimination.
Fill in a missing factor pair of 36.
Choose the first common multiple of 6 and 8 from options and explain the choice.
activities.insight: Consolidates and checks the factor/multiple distinction, completeness, and the meaning of overlap once the ideas have been built.

checkQuestion: Is 97 a prime number? Decide, and then explain how you know for certain — what did you have to check, and how did you know when you could stop checking?
checkAnswer: Yes, 97 is prime. A child reasoning correctly checks for factors other than 1 and 97 by testing divisibility by primes up to √97 (≈ 9.8) — 2, 3, 5, 7 — finds none divide it, and concludes it has exactly two factors. The key reasoning is WHY they can stop at ~10 (beyond that, a factor would pair with one already checked).
